# GOOG (Alphabet Inc.) — Value Investor Note

## Circle of Competence
Alphabet's economic engine is straightforward at the level that matters: sell attention and intent (Search, YouTube) to advertisers, at massive scale, with a data-driven flywheel that keeps improving targeting. That is well within a value investor's circle of competence, the same way Buffett came around to Apple as 'a consumer products company with a great moat' rather than a tech bet. The genuine competence-stretching question - identical to the one facing every incumbent search/media business right now - is how fast generative-AI interfaces displace the query-and-ten-blue-links model, and whether Alphabet's own AI products capture that shift or get disintermediated by it. That is a live, unresolved debate, not a settled fact.

## Moat & Durability — Score 8/10
Search's ~90% share is reinforced by a genuine network effect (more usage -> better targeting -> more advertiser demand -> more revenue to reinvest in the product), plus Chrome/Android distribution and YouTube's video dominance - moats built over two decades that a well-funded challenger cannot simply out-spend into existence. Two things keep this from a 9-10: (1) generative-AI answer engines are a structurally different threat than prior search challengers (Bing, DuckDuckGo) because they can shrink the number of ad-monetizable clicks even if Alphabet keeps its 'share of search,' and (2) the DOJ's search-monopoly finding leaves real remedy risk on the table (data-sharing mandates, default-placement restrictions, potential ad-tech separation) that is outside management's control. Cloud (GCP) is a credible but distant-third moat, riding the same AI wave as everyone else rather than leading it.

## Management & Capital Allocation
A 48.7% ROE on debt/equity of roughly 18.9% reflects a core ad business that still earns extraordinary returns on capital without leverage doing the work - real operating strength. But the packet's most important number here is the FCF yield: just 0.54% against a $4.2T market cap, a striking gap from a company historically famous for throwing off cash. That says essentially all of operating cash flow is currently being reinvested into AI infrastructure capex. This is a rational bet if the spend is disciplined and earns a real return; it is capital destruction if it is an arms-race reflex. This packet has no way to distinguish the two, no buyback/dividend cadence, and no stock-based-comp or insider-alignment data - all are unknowns, not verified positives.

## Predictability
Revenue growth of 24.2% and an operating margin of 34.0% both say the core franchise is healthy today. But earnings predictability is currently impaired: forward P/E (23.3x) sits above trailing P/E (17.3x) - the market is pricing a earnings decline even as revenue grows, most likely a combination of fading one-time gains in trailing GAAP net income and rising depreciation from the capex build-out. Combined with a near-zero FCF yield and a null momentum thesis in this packet, that fails Munger's 'easy decision' bar this year, even though the business model itself remains simple to understand. Momentum context: +68.9% over 12 months but -13.8% over 3 months and -7.1% over 1 month, with RSI14 at 62.5 (neutral-to-firm) and price still +4.3% above the 200-day average - a strong long-run trend that has cooled sharply in the near term, consistent with the market digesting both the AI-disruption question and the capex-driven FCF compression.

## Inversion — How an Owner Loses Money From Here
1. **AI disintermediates Search faster than Alphabet monetizes AI**: generative answer engines shrink click volume and ad economics structurally, while Alphabet's own AI products (AI Overviews, Gemini) cannibalize legacy Search revenue without fully replacing it, all while capex stays elevated regardless of the outcome.
2. **Antitrust remedies bite**: the DOJ search-monopoly case's remedies phase forces structural change (data-sharing mandates, default-placement restrictions, ad-tech separation) that permanently impairs unit economics in a way management cannot fully offset.
3. **The capex cycle over-builds**: AI infrastructure spend outruns realized demand, keeping FCF depressed for years past what the current 0.54% FCF yield already implies, without the earnings growth needed to justify the investment - a value trap disguised as a growth story.

## Valuation
The packet gives market cap ($4.201T), trailing P/E (17.27x), forward P/E (23.30x), EV/EBITDA (23.69x), and FCF yield (0.54%) but not share count or share price directly. Backing into per-share terms using an approximate ~11.9B combined share count (a modeling assumption, not sourced from the packet) implies a current price near $353/share, trailing EPS near $20.44, forward EPS near $15.15, and FCF/share near just $1.90 - a striking gap versus GAAP earnings that itself is a valuation red flag.

Normalizing owner earnings by blending trailing and forward EPS and haircutting for the capex-driven FCF gap gives roughly $18/share in normalized owner earnings. Applying a two-stage range:
- **Low case** (16x, reflecting real AI-disruption and antitrust-remedy risk): ~$288/share.
- **High case** (20x, if the AI capex build-out pays off and the ad/cloud franchise proves resilient): ~$360/share.

Midpoint ~$324/share vs. an implied current price of ~$353/share gives a margin of safety of roughly **-9%** - the market is asking a value investor to pay slightly above a reasonable owner-earnings estimate for a business whose near-term free cash flow has been almost entirely absorbed by an unproven capex cycle. That is a real quality business at a full-to-rich price, not a bargain.

## The Cloning Caveat
This is an unusually broad and, in one case, unusually loud buy signal. Warren Buffett/Berkshire Hathaway opened a new position in Q1 2026 (0.39% of portfolio) and then increased it 658% in Q2 2026 to 2.79% of portfolio - a dramatic, fast build for a manager who almost never buys technology and who is famously slow to build conviction. Duan Yongping (H&H International, a long-time Buffett admirer) added 99.7% to 2.65% of portfolio over the same window. Seth Klarman (Baupost) and Chris Hohn (TCI) both added across two consecutive quarters, Bill Nygren (Oakmark, a quality-focused value investor) added 118%, and Christopher Bloomstran (Semper Augustus, a deep-value shop) opened a new position. Several smaller/token additions (Yacktman, First Pacific, Mairs & Power) round out the list. This is genuine, weight-of-evidence corroboration from a cluster of disciplined value investors, led by the most conservative capital allocator in the business making a rare and rapid tech commitment - but per the cloning caveat, it corroborates the moat-and-quality thesis, not the price. None of it changes the packet's own math: near-zero FCF yield and a forward P/E above the trailing P/E.

## Verdict
**Watch, conviction 6/10.** Alphabet is an understandable, durably-moated, exceptionally high-ROE business that superinvestors - Buffett most emphatically - are voting for with real capital. But this packet's own numbers (a 0.54% FCF yield, forward P/E above trailing P/E, and a margin of safety around -9% against a conservative owner-earnings estimate) say the price is not offering a value investor's cushion right now. The disciplined read is to watch closely, own it if already held via other exposure, and look for a pullback or for the capex cycle to prove out in cash-flow terms before sizing a fresh position - buying a wonderful business is still supposed to happen at a fair price, and today's price, on this packet's evidence, is full.
momentum_thesis: GOOG's 12-month tape is still strong (+68.9%) but the trailing quarter has rolled over hard, down 13.8% over 3 months and 7.1% over the last month, so the name is now round-tripping gains rather than extending them. RSI14 at 62.5 is neutral-to-firm, not oversold, which means the pullback hasn't reset positioning and there's no technical spring loaded for a bounce. Price is holding just 4.3% above the 200DMA — a thin cushion after a double-digit 3-month drawdown — so another leg down puts the long-term trend line in play. There's no short-covering fuel to catch a reversal: short ratio is a scant 2.35 days to cover and the squeeze component of the score is a flat zero, while put/call OI at 0.79 shows only mild call-side positioning, not conviction. The superinvestor buying (Buffett's new Q1 stake scaled up 658% in Q2, plus Klarman, Hohn/TCI, and Maverick adding across both quarters) is real and broad, but it reads as value accumulation into the price weakness, not a momentum tailwind — this crowd buys dips on fundamentals, they don't chase strength, so it's a valuation floor argument more than a trend-continuation one.
